rw: Conflict management means helping people settle disagreements. Listening to both sides and suggesting a compromise is the classic approach, and it keeps the team working together.

ww.Fierce competition: Fierce competition pits people against each other to win. A third person who listens to both sides and proposes a compromise is trying to help, not to beat anyone.
ww.Manipulation of others: Manipulation means influencing people through deceit or pressure for your own gain. Listening openly to both sides and suggesting a fair compromise is honest and transparent.
ww.Avoidance of the issue: Avoidance means staying out of a conflict and hoping it fades. Here the third person steps in, listens and proposes a compromise, which is the opposite of avoiding.

rw: Stress management means using healthy strategies, such as planning, exercise, breaks and talking to someone, to handle pressure. It keeps people productive and well.

ww.Blaming coworkers for deadlines that are: Blaming coworkers for missed deadlines does nothing to manage stress. It harms relationships and leaves the cause of the pressure unaddressed.
ww.Ignoring problems until they disappear: Ignoring problems rarely makes them disappear, and the stress usually grows. Stress management means facing pressure with healthy strategies.
ww.Taking on more work just to feel busy at: Piling on extra work just to feel busy adds to the load and burns people out. Real stress management lowers pressure, not raises it.

rw: Prioritizing tasks makes a heavy workload manageable, and short breaks restore energy and focus. Together they are the most effective way to ease stress.

ww.Ignoring deadlines until the last day: Ignoring deadlines until the last day piles up work and raises stress. Starting early and pacing the work lowers pressure much more.
ww.Working without any sleep at night for a: Going a week without sleep damages health, focus and mood. It raises stress and the chance of mistakes instead of reducing them.
ww.Skipping meals to finish tasks faster ea: Skipping meals to save time lowers energy and concentration. The tiredness it causes makes work slower and stress higher.

rw: Resilience is the ability to recover from setbacks and adapt. Resilient people bounce back from failure, learn from it and keep going.

ww.Avoiding all challenges that come along: Avoiding all challenges is the opposite of resilience. Resilient people face difficulties instead of running from them.
ww.Giving up when things get hard for you a: Giving up when things get hard shows a lack of resilience. Resilience means persisting and finding another way forward.
ww.Never making any mistakes at work or at: Nobody avoids all mistakes, so resilience cannot mean perfection. It means recovering and learning when mistakes or setbacks occur.

rw: Resilience is bouncing back from a setback and trying again. The salesperson lost a big deal but chose to learn from it and continue.

ww.Delaying tasks: Delaying tasks is procrastination. The salesperson is learning and trying again, which is the opposite of putting things off.
ww.Indifference: Indifference means not caring about the result. Choosing to learn from the loss shows that the outcome mattered.
ww.Aggression: Aggression means hostile behavior toward others. Learning from a loss and trying again is a constructive response.

rw: Entrepreneurs create new businesses, jobs and ideas. They bring innovation, give people work and drive economic growth.

ww.Setting taxes for all firms in the natio: Taxes are set by governments, not entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurs start and grow businesses within that system.
ww.Printing money for the state and its peo: Money is printed by the state's central authorities. An entrepreneur's contribution is creating businesses and products, not currency.
ww.Regulating trade between nations and fir: Regulating trade is a job for governments. Entrepreneurs take part in markets rather than regulate them.

rw: Start-up capital is the money needed to start a business, covering equipment, inventory, licenses and early expenses. It may come from savings, loans or investors.

ww.The profit earned in the first year: Profit earned in the first year comes after the business is running. Start-up capital is needed before that, to begin operating.
ww.The tax paid by a new business each year: Taxes are paid out of earnings once trading. They are not the funds needed to launch a business.
ww.The owner's salary for the first year: The owner's salary is a cost of running the business. Start-up capital is the money used to get it started.

rw: Bootstrapping means starting a business with little outside money, mostly the founder's savings and early sales. It keeps ownership and control with the founder.

ww.Raising millions of dollars from many ou: Raising millions from many outside investors is the opposite of bootstrapping. Bootstrapping avoids outside money.
ww.Borrowing a large sum from a large bank: Borrowing a large sum from a bank is debt financing. Bootstrapping relies on the founder's own resources.
ww.Selling the whole business outright to a: Selling the whole business to a competitor is an exit. It is not a way of starting up.

rw: Personal savings and bank loans raise money without giving up ownership. A bank loan must be repaid, but the lender does not take a share of the firm.

ww.Merging with a rival company: Merging with a rival combines two companies. It is not a way to raise funds for a start-up, and ownership would be shared.
ww.Giving away half of profits: Giving away half of profits means giving up a large share of the gains. That would not leave the founder with full ownership of the returns.
ww.Selling a large share of the firm: Selling a large share of the firm means giving up ownership. The question asks for ways to keep full ownership.

rw: A business model describes how a business creates, delivers and earns money from value. It explains who the customers are and how revenue comes in.

ww.A large building where products are made: A building where products are made is a factory. A business model describes how a business operates and earns money.
ww.A person who advertises a product to the: A person who advertises a product is a promoter or spokesperson. A business model is a plan for how the whole business works.
ww.A small version of a product that is mad: A small version of a product for tests is a prototype. A business model is about how the business makes money.

rw: A free app that earns from ads is an advertising-based business model. Users pay nothing, and advertisers pay to reach them.

ww.A nonprofit model that has no revenue at: Nonprofit models still have revenue, such as donations. This start-up earns money from ads, so it does not fit.
ww.A subscription model charging monthly fe: A subscription model charges users a regular fee. The app is free, so users are not paying.
ww.A franchise model licensing the brand to: A franchise model licenses a brand to others. The start-up is earning from ads, not from licensing.

rw: An MVP is a basic version of a product used to test an idea with real users. It lets a start-up learn quickly and cheaply before building more.

ww.A product that has no features at all an: An MVP has just enough features to be useful and tested. A product with no features and no use would teach nothing.
ww.The final perfect version of a product,: The final perfect version is the goal, not the MVP. An MVP is released early so the team can learn.
ww.A product sold only to investors and to: An MVP is meant for real users, so it is shown to the public. Restricting it to investors and banks defeats the purpose of testing.

rw: A pitch is a short presentation that explains a business idea to investors or customers. Its goal is to win support, funding or sales.

ww.A tax form that a firm files with the go: A tax form reports income to the government. A pitch is a presentation of an idea.
ww.A list of all the expenses of the firm f: A list of expenses is a budget. A pitch persuades an audience.
ww.A legal contract signed by two parties w: A contract between two parties is a legal agreement. A pitch comes before any deal and aims to persuade.

rw: A strong investor pitch covers the problem, the solution, the market and how the business makes money. These show that the idea is real and can earn a return.

ww.Only a long list of competitors' names a: A list of competitors' names and prices covers only one small part. An investor wants the problem, solution, market and revenue plan too.
ww.Only the founder's hobbies and interests: The founder's hobbies are not relevant to the business case. Investors want to see a plan for the business.
ww.Only the color of the logo and the name: A logo color and brand name are small details. The pitch needs substance about the business.

rw: Scaling means growing revenue faster than costs. As the business expands, each extra sale brings in more profit.

ww.Reducing the number of customers: Reducing customers would shrink the business. Scaling means growing it.
ww.Weighing products on a big scale: Weighing products on a scale is a literal use of the word. In business, scaling means growth.
ww.Keeping the business the same size: Keeping the business the same size is the opposite of scaling. Scaling means expanding.

rw: Growing too fast can use up cash because costs rise before payments come in. The firm may also be unable to meet demand, which harms customers.

ww.Having a stronger brand overnight with n: A stronger brand overnight with no extra cost is a benefit, not a risk. Growing too fast usually costs more.
ww.Having more choices of suppliers in the: More supplier choices are an advantage. It is not a risk of fast growth.
ww.Having too many satisfied customers to c: Having too many satisfied customers is a good problem. The real risk of fast growth is running short of resources.

rw: The current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities. It shows whether a firm can pay debts due within a year.

ww.Profit margin: Profit margin shows the share of sales kept as profit. It does not measure the ability to pay short-term debts.
ww.Return on equity: Return on equity measures profit relative to owners' investment. It does not test short-term debt cover.
ww.Inventory turnover: Inventory turnover shows how quickly stock sells. It does not measure short-term debt ability.

rw: Return on investment is the gain from an investment relative to its cost. It shows how efficiently money is used.

ww.The total amount invested in the venture: The total amount invested is the cost of the investment. ROI compares the gain with that cost.
ww.The tax paid on an investment during the: Tax paid is a payment to the government. ROI measures the return on money invested.
ww.The time needed to repay a loan from a b: Time to repay a loan is the payback period or loan term. ROI measures the gain relative to cost.

rw: ROI equals the extra profit divided by the cost. $3,000 divided by $20,000 is 0.15, so the annual ROI is 15%.

ww.6.7%: 6.7% does not match the numbers. ROI is the annual profit divided by the cost, $3,000 over $20,000, which is 15%.
ww.60%: 60% is far too high. Dividing $3,000 by $20,000 gives 0.15, or 15%.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 is a dollar amount, not a percentage. ROI is the profit as a share of the cost, which is 15%.

rw: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It shows the funds available to run day-to-day operations.

ww.Total assets minus total liabilities: Total assets minus total liabilities is owner's equity. Working capital uses only current assets and current liabilities.
ww.Cash plus fixed assets of the firm now: Cash plus fixed assets is not working capital. Fixed assets are long-term and are not used in day-to-day operations.
ww.Revenue minus expenses of the firm for a: Revenue minus expenses is net income. Working capital is based on the balance sheet, not the income statement.

rw: A debt ratio measures the share of assets financed by debt. A higher ratio means more borrowing and more risk.

ww.How fast inventory sells each year: How fast inventory sells is inventory turnover. A debt ratio is about financing.
ww.How much cash is on hand each month: Cash on hand is a liquidity matter. A debt ratio is about debt.
ww.The share of sales kept as profit: The share of sales kept as profit is the profit margin. A debt ratio looks at assets and liabilities.

rw: The debt ratio is total liabilities divided by total assets. $60,000 divided by $150,000 is 0.40, or 40%.

ww.250%: 250% inverts the formula, assets over liabilities. The debt ratio is liabilities divided by assets.
ww.90%: 90% does not follow from the numbers. $60,000 divided by $150,000 is 0.40.
ww.60%: 60% uses the dollar figure of $60,000 as a percent. The ratio is liabilities divided by assets, or 40%.

rw: Inventory turnover is how many times inventory is sold and replaced in a period. A high figure means goods sell quickly.

ww.The profit from each product that a firm: The profit from each product is unit profit. Inventory turnover measures how often stock sells.
ww.The cost of storing inventory in a large: Storage cost is the carrying cost. Turnover measures how often stock is sold and replaced.
ww.The number of products held in a warehou: The number of products held is the inventory level. Turnover is about the rate of selling.

rw: Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory is $240,000 over $40,000, which is 6. Inventory sells and is replaced six times a year.

ww.200 times: 200 times is not what the numbers give. Turnover is cost of goods sold divided by average inventory, $240,000 over $40,000.
ww.280 times: 280 times adds the figures. The formula divides cost of goods sold by average inventory.
ww.0.17 times: 0.17 times turns the formula upside down. Turnover is cost of goods sold over average inventory, which is 6.

rw: Recruitment is finding and attracting qualified candidates for jobs. It builds the pool from which a hire is made.

ww.Paying employees each month for their ti: Paying employees is payroll. Recruitment is about bringing in new staff.
ww.Reviewing an employee's work each year t: Reviewing work to set a raise is a performance appraisal. Recruitment comes before someone is hired.
ww.Ending an employee's job at the firm for: Ending an employee's job is termination. Recruitment is the opposite, finding people to join.

rw: Asking whether someone plans to have children is unlawful. Family plans are not related to doing the job and could lead to discrimination.

ww.Are you legally allowed to work here?: Asking if someone is legally allowed to work in the country is lawful. Employers must confirm eligibility.
ww.Why are you interested in this job?: Asking why someone is interested in the job is lawful. It relates directly to the role.
ww.Can you do the essential job duties: Asking whether the person can do the essential job duties is lawful. It focuses on ability to do the work.

rw: A performance appraisal is a formal review of an employee's work. It gives feedback and sets goals for improvement.

ww.A review of company profits this year: A review of company profits is a financial review. An appraisal looks at an individual employee.
ww.A review of customer complaints made: A review of complaints concerns customers. An appraisal is about an employee's work.
ww.A review of the office layout plan: A review of the office layout is a facilities matter. It does not review a person's performance.

rw: Employee turnover is the rate at which employees leave and are replaced. A high rate is costly and may signal problems.

ww.The number of customers served each day: The number of customers served is a sales or traffic figure. Turnover is about staff.
ww.The rate at which sales grow from year t: Sales growth is a financial figure. Turnover concerns people leaving.
ww.The rate at which profits rise in a grow: Profit growth is a financial measure. Employee turnover counts departures.

rw: Turnover rate equals leavers divided by employees. 30 divided by 150 is 0.20, or 20%.

ww.30%: 30% takes the 30 leavers as a percent. Turnover is 30 divided by 150 employees.
ww.50%: 50% is too high. Thirty leavers out of 150 is one in five.
ww.5%: 5% is too low. Thirty out of 150 is 20 percent.

rw: Job rotation moves employees between different jobs to build skills. It prepares staff for more roles and keeps work interesting.

ww.Keeping staff in one job forever, each e: Keeping staff in one job forever is the opposite of rotation. Rotation moves people around.
ww.Cutting working hours for staff at the f: Cutting working hours is a scheduling change. It is not job rotation.
ww.Firing and then rehiring workers at the: Firing and rehiring is not rotation. Rotation moves current employees between roles.

rw: Diversity means differences among employees, such as background, age and experience. Different views can improve ideas and decisions.

ww.Having employees work alone in their own: Working alone in separate rooms is about layout. It does not describe differences among people.
ww.Having every employee do exactly the sam: Everyone doing the same task is uniformity. Diversity refers to differences.
ww.Hiring only people of one single age gro: Hiring only one age group reduces diversity. It is the opposite.

rw: A grievance procedure is a fair process for employees to raise and resolve complaints. It protects workers and helps firms fix problems.

ww.A schedule of pay days for the staff of: A schedule of pay days is a payroll calendar. A grievance procedure handles complaints.
ww.A list of company rules for the staff of: A list of company rules is a policy manual. A grievance procedure is a process.
ww.A way to fire workers with no notice, wh: Firing without notice is not a grievance procedure. It would be the cause of a grievance.

rw: A spreadsheet is used to organize and calculate data in rows and columns. It handles budgets, lists and charts.

ww.Designing company logos and signs for th: Designing logos is done with graphics software. A spreadsheet is for numbers.
ww.Sending video calls to team members acro: Video calls use conferencing software. A spreadsheet works with data in cells.
ww.Protecting computers from viruses and at: Protecting against viruses is the job of security software. A spreadsheet does not do that.

rw: SUM adds the numbers in a range of cells. It is the function used to total a column.

ww.ROUND: ROUND changes a number to a set number of decimal places. It does not add a column of numbers.
ww.COUNT: COUNT counts how many cells contain numbers. It does not add values.
ww.MAX: MAX finds the largest value in a range. It does not add them.

rw: Data backup is making copies of data to restore if the original is lost. It protects against failure, error and attack.

ww.Deleting old data that is no longer of a: Deleting old data is data disposal. A backup keeps copies.
ww.Encrypting passwords for the users of a: Encrypting passwords is a security measure. It is not the same as backing up data.
ww.Updating software on the computers of a: Updating software is maintenance. It does not copy data.

rw: Phishing is a scam that tricks people into revealing sensitive information, often through fake emails or sites. Attackers pose as trusted sources.

ww.A hobby of catching fish on a lake in th: Catching fish is a hobby. The similar spelling is a pun on fishing for information.
ww.A method of encrypting data so that only: Encrypting data protects it. Phishing is an attack that tricks people.
ww.A kind of spreadsheet used by firms in a: A kind of spreadsheet is not phishing. Phishing is a form of fraud.

rw: Not clicking and reporting it is the safe choice. It protects you and lets IT warn others.

ww.Click and log in now: Clicking and logging in on an unfamiliar link may give your password to a scammer. It could cost you your account.
ww.Forward it to coworkers: Forwarding it spreads the scam to coworkers. It could put them at risk.
ww.Reply with your password: Replying with your password gives it directly to the attacker. Never share passwords by email.

rw: Cloud computing uses remote servers on the internet to store and process data. Users can reach files from many devices.

ww.Storing data on paper in a filing cabine: Storing data on paper in a cabinet is physical storage. Cloud computing uses remote servers.
ww.Using only one computer in an office, ho: Using one computer for everything is local computing. Cloud computing spreads work over remote servers.
ww.Using computers without electricity or p: Computers need electricity. Cloud computing runs on servers elsewhere.

rw: Target marketing means aiming at a specific group, here serious athletes. It focuses efforts on the customers most likely to buy.

ww.Price fixing: Price fixing is an illegal agreement between rivals on prices. Aiming shoes at athletes is unrelated.
ww.Inventory control: Inventory control manages stock levels. The company is choosing customers, not managing stock.
ww.Mass production: Mass production makes large quantities. It does not describe aiming at a specific group.

rw: Branding creates a name or symbol that identifies a business's products. It sets them apart and builds recognition.

ww.Setting the price of products in the sho: Setting prices is pricing. Branding creates an identity.
ww.Counting products in a warehouse at year: Counting stock is inventory control. It does not give the firm an identity.
ww.Delivering goods to customers in vans ea: Delivering goods is distribution. Branding is about identity.

rw: Market research gathers information about customers and competitors. It helps a firm make informed decisions.

ww.Filing taxes for a firm at the end of a: Filing taxes is an accounting task. Market research collects information.
ww.Making products in a factory for the fir: Making products is production. Research gathers information.
ww.Printing flyers for a big sale at the lo: Printing flyers is advertising work. It is not research.

rw: Supply chain management coordinates the flow of goods from suppliers to customers. It includes sourcing, production, storage and delivery.

ww.Advertising goods in the news and on the: Advertising goods is promotion. Supply chain management moves goods.
ww.Setting prices for goods in stores that: Setting prices is pricing. Supply chain management coordinates the flow of goods.
ww.Hiring employees for the firm at its mai: Hiring is human resources. It is not supply chain management.

rw: Using more than one supplier spreads risk. If one is late, another can fill the gap.

ww.Rely on the same supplier: Relying on the same supplier leaves the risk in place. The factory would face the same delay again.
ww.Ignore the delay and wait: Ignoring a delay and waiting does not solve the problem. Production would stay at risk.
ww.Stop making the product: Stopping production loses sales. It does not fix the supply problem.

rw: Quality control means checking products to ensure they meet standards. It finds defects before products reach customers.

ww.Hiring workers for the factory floor of: Hiring workers is HR. Quality control checks products.
ww.Setting the price of products after a st: Setting prices is pricing. Quality control checks products meet standards.
ww.Promoting products on the radio and in p: Promoting products is marketing. Quality control is about checking output.

rw: A professional network is a group of contacts who share advice and opportunities. It can lead to jobs, mentors and partners.

ww.A computer network inside an office that: A computer network links devices. A professional network links people.
ww.A group of competitors in the same marke: Competitors are rivals. A professional network is a group of helpful contacts.
ww.A list of customers of the firm and thei: Customers and their orders are sales records. They are not a professional network.

rw: Admitting a mistake, fixing it and learning from it shows professionalism. It builds trust and prevents repeats.

ww.Hide it and hope no one notices: Hiding a mistake and hoping no one notices is dishonest. It can make the problem worse.
ww.Ignore it and just carry on as usual: Ignoring a mistake and carrying on leaves it unfixed. A professional takes responsibility.
ww.Blame a coworker for the error: Blaming a coworker is unfair and dishonest. It damages relationships.

rw: Differentiation means standing out through qualities such as freshness and local products. It lets the bakery compete without cutting prices.

ww.Imitating them: Imitating a chain means copying it. The bakery is offering something different.
ww.Closing down: Closing down is giving up. The bakery is competing with fresh, local products.
ww.Cost leadership: Cost leadership means having the lowest prices. The bakery says it cannot beat the chain on price.

rw: A tort is a civil wrong that causes harm to another person. The injured person can sue for compensation.

ww.A crime punished only by prison time in: A crime punished by prison is criminal. A tort is a civil wrong.
ww.A written agreement between two firms, s: A written agreement is a contract. A tort is a wrong.
ww.A tax paid to the state by a firm each y: A tax is a payment to the state. A tort is a civil wrong.

rw: Food poisoning from a restaurant is a civil wrong, which falls under tort law. The customer may sue for damages.

ww.Antitrust: Antitrust law concerns competition and monopolies. A food poisoning claim is about harm.
ww.Tax law: Tax law covers taxes. It does not apply to a harm claim.
ww.Labor law: Labor law covers workers' rights. It does not cover a customer's injury.

rw: A trade secret is confidential business information that gives a competitive edge. Examples include recipes and customer lists.

ww.A public record of a firm's yearly profi: A public record of profits is not secret. A trade secret is confidential.
ww.A government contract with a supplier of: A government contract is an agreement. It is not secret information.
ww.A tax deduction used by a firm to cut th: A tax deduction reduces a tax bill. It is not a trade secret.

rw: Taking a client list to a competitor is misuse of confidential business information. The employee may face legal action.

ww.A normal career move that employers expe: Taking a client list in breach of a confidentiality agreement is not a normal career move. It breaks legal duties.
ww.A sales promotion by a firm in a market: It is not a sales promotion. It is taking confidential information.
ww.A tax saving method used by a firm each: It is not a tax saving method. It is a breach of confidentiality.

rw: A non-compete agreement is a contract limiting an employee's ability to work for competitors after leaving. It protects the firm's secrets and clients.

ww.A rule about paid vacation days for the: Paid vacation rules are a matter of benefits. A non-compete agreement limits working for rivals.
ww.A promise never to quit a job at the fir: A promise never to quit is not a non-compete. It concerns what happens after leaving.
ww.A guarantee of a yearly raise in pay for: A guaranteed raise is a pay term. A non-compete limits future work.

rw: Arbitration is when a neutral person hears both sides and decides a dispute. The decision is often binding.

ww.One party decides the outcome alone, wit: If one party decides alone, it is not arbitration. A neutral person must decide.
ww.Two parties argue in front of a jury tha: A jury trial is a court case. Arbitration is private and done without a jury.
ww.A government agency sets the price for a: A government agency setting prices is regulation. It is not arbitration.

rw: Mediation is when a neutral person helps the parties reach their own agreement. The mediator guides talks but does not decide.

ww.A jury decides the dispute in a court of: A jury deciding in court is a trial. Mediation is a negotiation with help.
ww.A judge issues a binding decision after: A judge issuing a binding decision is a court ruling. Mediation does not impose a result.
ww.A neutral person imposes a ruling on bot: A neutral person imposing a ruling is arbitration. In mediation the parties decide.

rw: Mediation and arbitration are private and faster than court. They let partners settle without a lawsuit.

ww.A long jury trial in court: A long jury trial is public, slow and costly. It is not a quick, private option.
ww.Ignoring the dispute: Ignoring a dispute does not settle it. It often makes things worse.
ww.A public vote of staff: A public vote of staff is not a legal way to settle a dispute. It would not be binding.

rw: A statute of limitations is a deadline for bringing a legal claim. After it passes, the claim is usually barred.

ww.A cap on damages a court can award: A cap on damages limits what a court can award. The statute of limitations is a time limit.
ww.A limit on the number of witnesses: A limit on witnesses is a court procedure. It is not a time limit on claims.
ww.A limit on a lawyer's fees in a case: Limits on lawyers' fees are a separate rule. The statute of limitations is about time.

rw: An employment contract is an agreement that sets the terms of a job, such as pay and duties. It protects both employer and employee.

ww.A tax form for the workers of a firm to: A tax form is filed with the government. An employment contract is an agreement.
ww.A request for a large bank loan for a ne: A loan request goes to a bank. It is not an employment contract.
ww.A list of company products with the pric: A list of products and prices is a catalog. It is not a job agreement.

rw: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage, overtime and child labor rules. It protects workers' pay and hours.

ww.Rules for food labels on goods in stores: Food labels are covered by food safety laws. The Fair Labor Standards Act covers work.
ww.Rules for advertising of goods on air: Advertising rules are consumer protection laws. The FLSA covers workers.
ww.Rules for stock trading and broker dutie: Stock trading is regulated by securities law. The FLSA is about labor.

rw: Child labor laws limit the work young people may do, especially hazardous jobs. Machinery is banned for a 14-year-old.

ww.Securities law: Securities law covers stock trading. A teen on dangerous machinery is a labor issue.
ww.Copyright law: Copyright law protects creative works. It does not govern workplace safety.
ww.Antitrust law: Antitrust law concerns competition. It does not apply to a teen's job.

rw: Product liability is a seller's responsibility for harm caused by defective products. Injured buyers may seek compensation.

ww.A tax placed on products sold by a firm: A tax on products is a sales or excise tax. Product liability concerns harm.
ww.A rule about shelf size for goods displa: Shelf size is a store rule. Product liability is about defective products.
ww.A buyer's duty to pay on time for goods: A buyer's duty to pay is a payment duty. It is not product liability.

rw: The manufacturer, and possibly the seller, may be liable for a defective product. A design flaw is the maker's responsibility.

ww.No one, because accidents are normal: Accidents are not just normal when a flaw causes harm. Someone can be liable.
ww.Only the government of the state itself: The government of the state is not the party responsible. The maker and seller are.
ww.Only the injured user of the blender: The user is not at fault when a design flaw causes injury. Blame lies with the seller or maker.

rw: A persuasive message is designed to influence what an audience thinks or does. It uses reasons and appeals to win support.

ww.A message that only lists facts and asks: A message that only lists facts and asks nothing is informative. A persuasive message aims to influence.
ww.A message that forces compliance from al: Forcing compliance is coercion. Persuasion lets people choose.
ww.A message that hides its aim from the pe: Hiding its aim is deception. A persuasive message states its purpose.

rw: A short line that connects to the reader's problem shows relevance quickly. It encourages the reader to continue.

ww.A long paragraph about the company's his: A long history paragraph is dull and off topic. It does not grab the reader.
ww.A list of every product the firm has sol: A list of every product is overwhelming. It does not connect to the reader's need.
ww.A generic greeting with no clear purpose: A generic greeting is forgettable. It does not give a reason to keep reading.

rw: Body language is gestures, posture and expressions that communicate feelings. It can support or contradict spoken words.

ww.The written notes of a meeting, typed up: Written notes of a meeting are minutes. Body language is nonverbal.
ww.The words spoken aloud by the people in: Spoken words are verbal. Body language uses movement and expression.
ww.The volume of a phone call between two o: Volume is part of tone of voice. Body language is physical.

rw: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in a business's decisions. This includes owners, employees, customers, suppliers and the community.

ww.Only the competitors of the business, si: Competitors are not the only stakeholders. A stakeholder is anyone affected by the business.
ww.Only the owner of the business, since no: The owner is only one stakeholder. Others are affected too.
ww.Only the managers of the business, since: Managers are stakeholders, but not the only ones. Many groups have an interest.

rw: Being clear, honest and compassionate, and explaining next steps, respects the people affected. It helps them plan.

ww.Send a vague email to everyone and then: A vague email and avoiding questions leaves people confused. It is not respectful.
ww.Announce it publicly with no warning to: Announcing layoffs publicly with no warning is harsh. Those affected deserve notice and care.
ww.Blame the employees for the decision tha: Blaming employees is unfair. The decision was made by leaders.

rw: Knowing your audience lets you tailor the message to their needs and level. It keeps them interested and helps them understand.

ww.You can use the same talk for everyone w: One talk for everyone ignores differences. Audiences vary in knowledge and interests.
ww.You can avoid preparing at all, since it: Presenters must prepare. Knowing the audience guides the preparation.
ww.You can speak as fast as possible so it: Speaking fast does not help. It makes the message hard to follow.

rw: A line chart shows how a value changes over time. It suits sales over twelve months.

ww.A staff list: A staff list is a list of names. It shows no sales change.
ww.A pie chart: A pie chart shows parts of a whole. It does not show change over time well.
ww.A store photo: A store photo shows a place. It does not show trends in sales.

rw: An elevator pitch is a short, persuasive summary of an idea delivered in about 30 seconds. It is named for a short ride.

ww.A price list posted on the wall of an el: A price list on an elevator wall is not a pitch. An elevator pitch is a short speech.
ww.A long report presented to investors ove: A long report over hours is the opposite of an elevator pitch. It is meant to be short.
ww.A complaint about a building and how its: A complaint about a building is not a pitch. An elevator pitch promotes an idea.

rw: Revenue is monthly fee times months. $20 times 36 months is $720.

ww.$60: $60 is only three months of fees. The customer stays three years, which is 36 months.
ww.$2,160: $2,160 treats the fee as $60 a month. The fee is $20, so the total is $720.
ww.$240: $240 is one year of fees. The customer stays three years, so $720.

rw: Service recovery is actions taken to fix a problem and regain a customer's trust. Done well, it can build loyalty.

ww.Raising prices for everyone after a sing: Raising prices for everyone after one complaint is unfair. It does not fix the problem.
ww.Blaming the customer for the problem in: Blaming the customer damages the relationship. It is not recovery.
ww.Ignoring a complaint until it fades away: Ignoring a complaint lets the customer stay unhappy. It does not recover trust.

rw: Apologizing, replacing the meal quickly and adding a small gesture fixes the problem and shows care. This is good service recovery.

ww.Walk away without saying a single word t: Walking away without a word is rude. It leaves the diner without help.
ww.Tell the diner to eat what was served, s: Telling the diner to eat the wrong meal ignores the error. It is poor service.
ww.Charge extra for the correct meal that w: Charging extra for the correct meal is unfair, since the error was the restaurant's. It would anger the diner.

rw: Net Promoter Score measures how likely customers are to recommend a business. It is a common gauge of loyalty and satisfaction.

ww.A measure of employee turnover rates ove: Employee turnover is a staff measure. NPS is about customers.
ww.A measure of profit, found by subtractin: Profit is revenue minus costs. NPS measures recommendation.
ww.A measure of inventory levels held in th: Inventory levels are an operations figure. NPS measures customer loyalty.

rw: First-contact resolution means problems are solved the first time the customer asks. It saves time and raises satisfaction.

ww.It lets staff skip any follow-up with th: First-contact resolution does not mean skipping follow-up. It means solving the issue the first time.
ww.It makes calls last as long as possible: Long calls are not the aim. Solving problems quickly is.
ww.It removes the need for any service staf: Service staff are still needed. Resolution is about doing the job well.

rw: The opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. By studying, the student gave up $90 she could have earned.

ww.Nothing, because studying is free: Studying is free in money terms, but time has value. The student gave up $90 of pay.
ww.The total price of the exam itself: The price of the exam is not what she gave up by studying. Opportunity cost is the next best use of time.
ww.The cost of the textbook itself: The textbook cost is an out-of-pocket expense. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative.

rw: A substitute good is a product that can replace another. If one gets pricier, buyers may switch to the other.

ww.A product that is made abroad only: A product made abroad is an import. A substitute is something that can replace another.
ww.A product used together with another: A product used together with another is a complement. A substitute replaces.
ww.A product that no one ever wants: A product no one wants has no demand. It is not a substitute.

rw: When coffee gets more expensive, some buyers switch to tea. Demand for tea rises.

ww.It is zero: Demand for tea would not drop to zero. Many people still drink tea.
ww.It falls: Demand for tea would not fall. Tea is a substitute for coffee.
ww.No change: Prices of substitutes affect demand. A rise in coffee's price changes tea demand.

rw: A complementary good is used together with another. Examples are printers and ink, or cereal and milk.

ww.A product sold only in other countries: A product sold only abroad is not a complement. A complement is used with another good.
ww.A product that stands in for another: A product that stands in for another is a substitute. Complements go together.
ww.A product that is given away for free: A free product is not a complement. A complement is defined by use with another good.

rw: Perfect competition has many sellers of identical products and easy entry. No single seller can set the price.

ww.A market with one dominant seller who ca: One dominant seller describes a monopoly. Perfect competition has many sellers.
ww.A market with only a few large sellers w: A few large sellers describe an oligopoly. Perfect competition has many.
ww.A market controlled by government rules: A market with government price limits is regulated. Perfect competition is free of such control.

rw: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large sellers. Firms watch each other and can influence price.

ww.A market with no sellers and no buyers: A market with no sellers and no buyers has no trade. It is not an oligopoly.
ww.A market with thousands of sellers of on: Thousands of sellers describe perfect or monopolistic competition. An oligopoly has few.
ww.A market with just one seller and no riv: One seller with no rivals is a monopoly. An oligopoly has a few sellers.

rw: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price that can be charged. Governments use it to keep goods affordable.

ww.A legal minimum price that can be charge: A legal minimum price is a price floor. A ceiling sets a maximum.
ww.A tax added on to the prices of goods: A tax added to prices is a different policy. A ceiling is a price limit.
ww.The highest price a seller wants to char: The highest price a seller wants to charge is the seller's choice. A ceiling is set by law.

rw: A price ceiling below equilibrium holds the price too low. Demand exceeds supply, causing a shortage.

ww.A balance: A balance would mean supply equals demand. A ceiling below equilibrium prevents that.
ww.A surplus: A surplus is more supplied than demanded. A ceiling below equilibrium causes the opposite.
ww.Higher supply: Supply does not rise under a lower price. A ceiling reduces what sellers want to offer.

rw: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. It raises their price and protects local producers.

ww.A total ban on all trade: A total ban on trade is an embargo. A tariff is a tax.
ww.A tax on exported goods: A tax on exports is an export duty. A tariff is usually on imports.
ww.A discount on imports: A discount on imports is a subsidy. A tariff raises the price.

rw: Domestic steel producers benefit because imports are more expensive. They can sell more at higher prices.

ww.Consumers of steel goods: Consumers of steel goods pay higher prices because of a tariff. They are harmed.
ww.Foreign steel producers: Foreign producers lose sales because their steel costs more. They do not benefit.
ww.Steel-using manufacturers: Steel-using manufacturers pay more for steel. They lose out.

rw: Comparative advantage is the ability to produce at a lower opportunity cost than others. It explains why trade benefits both sides.

ww.A ban on imports of goods from other nat: A ban on imports is a trade barrier. Comparative advantage is about efficiency.
ww.The ability to produce everything at a l: Producing everything cheaper is absolute advantage. Comparative advantage is about opportunity cost.
ww.The largest army in a region of the worl: The largest army is military strength. It has nothing to do with trade.

rw: A recession is a period of declining economic activity lasting several months. Output, jobs and income fall.

ww.A time when all prices fall to zero as d: Prices do not fall to zero in a recession. It is a fall in activity.
ww.A period of rapid growth and low unemplo: Rapid growth and low unemployment describe a boom. A recession is the opposite.
ww.A one-day stock market dip that soon rec: A one-day dip is a market fluctuation. A recession lasts months.

rw: Privately asking if they want to talk and listening shows care and respect. It reflects emotional intelligence.

ww.Joke about it in front of the team right: Joking in front of the team could embarrass the coworker. It shows no empathy.
ww.Ignore it completely and move on with th: Ignoring the coworker misses a chance to help. Emotional intelligence notices feelings.
ww.Tell others about it as soon as the meet: Telling others breaks trust. It would worsen the coworker's feelings.

rw: Self-awareness is recognizing your own emotions and how they affect your behavior. It helps you respond wisely.

ww.Predicting what other people will do bef: Predicting what others will do is a different skill. Self-awareness is about yourself.
ww.Avoiding stressful situations whenever i: Avoiding stress is not awareness. Self-awareness means understanding your own reactions.
ww.Hiding your feelings from everyone so em: Hiding feelings is suppression. Self-awareness means recognizing them.

rw: Constructive feedback is specific, respectful input meant to help someone improve. It focuses on actions and gives ways to do better.

ww.Praise that has no details or any real s: Praise with no detail does not help someone improve. Constructive feedback is specific.
ww.Harsh criticism of a person's character,: Harsh criticism of character before the team humiliates. Constructive feedback is respectful.
ww.Silence about problems in the hope that: Silence about problems leaves them unsolved. Feedback should be shared.

rw: Praising what is clear and suggesting cost data is specific, respectful and helpful. It shows how to improve.

ww.Do better next time, since this one was: 'Do better next time' is vague. It does not say what to improve.
ww.Your report was bad and it needs to be d: Saying the report is bad with no reasons is unhelpful. It discourages.
ww.You never do anything right, and I doubt: Attacking the person is personal criticism. It does not help improve.

rw: A USP is what makes a business different from its competitors. It gives customers a reason to choose it.

ww.The legal form of the business, such as: The legal form is a structure choice. A USP is about difference.
ww.A daily schedule of employees and who wo: An employee schedule is an operations tool. A USP is a marketing idea.
ww.A list of the business's expenses, with: A list of expenses is a financial record. A USP is not about costs.

rw: Ethically sourced beans and a quiet study space make the cafe different. This is its unique selling proposition.

ww.Its tax filing for last year: A tax filing is a legal document. The cafe's promise is about what makes it special.
ww.Its lease agreement and rent: A lease and rent are property costs. They do not describe what sets the cafe apart.
ww.Its balance sheet for the year: A balance sheet shows assets and liabilities. It is not a selling point.

rw: Studying customers and competitors before launching shows if there is demand. It reduces the risk of starting.

ww.Guessing what customers want, based on t: Guessing from the owner's taste is risky. Research uses evidence.
ww.Copying a competitor exactly, down to th: Copying a competitor exactly gives no reason to choose you. Research helps find a gap.
ww.Skipping planning and starting to sell a: Skipping planning risks mistakes. Research comes first.

rw: Checking permits and surveying likely customers shows whether the truck can operate legally and has demand. It is a sound first step.

ww.Buy a big truck without researching firs: Buying a big truck without research risks wasted money. Research should come first.
ww.Set prices at random without any researc: Random prices could lose money or customers. Pricing should be based on costs and demand.
ww.Open in any location without any plan: Opening anywhere without a plan may miss customers or break rules. Planning is needed.

rw: A franchise is the right to operate a business using another company's brand and system. The franchisee pays fees and follows the franchisor's rules.

ww.A special tax that is paid by large comp: A special tax is a tax. A franchise is a right to operate a brand.
ww.A business owned by the government and r: A government-run business is a public enterprise. A franchise is privately owned.
ww.A store that sells used goods at low pri: A store selling used goods is a thrift store. It is not a franchise by itself.

rw: A venture capitalist is an investor who funds new businesses in exchange for ownership. They aim for high returns when the firm grows.

ww.A banker who lends to homeowners using t: A banker lending against a house is a mortgage lender. A venture capitalist funds start-ups.
ww.A government regulator that enforces tra: A regulator enforces rules. A venture capitalist invests.
ww.A supplier of raw materials to many fact: A supplier provides materials. A venture capitalist provides funding.

rw: Break-even is where total revenue equals total costs. At that point there is no profit and no loss.

ww.Where costs are zero for the firm: Costs do not go to zero at break-even. They equal revenue.
ww.Where profit is highest for the firm: Highest profit is a different point. Break-even has zero profit.
ww.Where sales are zero for the firm: Zero sales means a loss equal to fixed costs. It is not break-even.

rw: Each item earns $8 above its cost. $8,000 of fixed costs divided by $8 is 1,000 items to break even.

ww.667 items: 667 items does not match the formula. Break-even is fixed costs divided by profit per item, $8,000 over $8.
ww.8,000 items: 8,000 items uses fixed costs as a number of items. Divide by the $8 profit per item.
ww.400 items: 400 items is too low. $8,000 divided by $8 profit per item is 1,000.

rw: A budget variance is the difference between budgeted and actual amounts. It shows where spending or revenue differed from plan.

ww.A list of rules that staff must follow a: A list of rules is a policy. A budget variance is a difference in numbers.
ww.A type of insurance that a firm buys for: Insurance protects against loss. A variance compares budget and actual.
ww.A chart of sales made by the firm each q: A chart of sales is a sales report. A variance compares budget and actual.

rw: Net income is revenue minus all expenses. It is the profit left after costs.

ww.Assets minus liabilities: Assets minus liabilities is owner's equity. Net income is a profit figure.
ww.Revenue before any costs: Revenue before costs is gross revenue. Net income is what remains.
ww.Cash minus all debts owed: Cash minus debts is a net cash position. Net income comes from the income statement.
